comment_box: On behalf of Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, please see the attached letter urging the rescission of this proposed rule.
text:
===== FILE 20593__1.pdf =====
September 3, 2025  
 
The Honorable Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Undersecretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Attention: Reproductive Health Services, 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AS31) 
 
Dear Dr. Lieberman: 
 
Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America, is the largest women’s Zionist and 
Jewish women’s organization in the United States, with nearly 300,000 members in nearly every 
congressional district, and more than 3,000 members who are current or retired healthcare 
professionals. Hadassah champions protections for women’s and public health and supports 
access to the full continuum of reproductive health care, including stabilizing emergency 
treatments such as abortion. Hadassah strongly opposes the U.S. Department of Veterans 
Affairs’ (VA) proposed rule (RIN 2900-AS31) on Reproductive Health Services, which will lead 
to worse physical and mental health outcomes for veterans, including survivors of sexual 
assault, jeopardize the life, health and future fertility of pregnant people, and place unfair 
financial burdens on women servicemembers and veterans.  
 
The VA’s proposed rule,1 reinstates the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling, 
eliminating exceptions for rape, incest and the health of the mother. According to the VA’s own 
guidance, the Veteran’s Medical Benefits Package should include care and services that 
“prevent future health problems” and “enhance […] quality of life.”2 However, if the proposed 
rule is promulgated and implemented, it will jeopardize the health, well-being and fertility 
capacity of veterans, in direct conflict with these health benefits. This is especially devastating 
given the sacrifices our veterans and their families have made to serve and protect our country. 
It is our responsibility to protect the freedoms, rather than interfere with their right to access 
quality and safe reproductive health care. As the largest integrated health system in the country, 
restrictions on access to reproductive health care in the Veterans Health System will be 
devastating for the two million female veterans3 who have served our country, particularly the 
43% of women veterans using VA health care who are of reproductive age.4  
 
 
1 Reproductive Health Services; Department of Veterans Affairs 2025, 90 Fed. Reg. 36415 
2 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. About VA health benefits. https://www.va.gov/health-care/about-
va-health-benefits/.  
3 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Women Veterans Health Care. 
https://www.womenshealth.va.gov/materials-and-resources/facts-and-statistics.asp  
4 Coffey, M. (2023, August 29). Maternal Health Summit: Perinatal care for Veterans. VA News. 
https://news.va.gov/123157/maternal-health-summit-perinatal-care-veterans/  

We strongly encourage the VA to rescind this proposed rule and leave in place the March 2024 
rule finalizing the September 2022 Interim Final Rule (IFR), which allows for abortion care to be 
provided in cases of rape, incest and to protect the health of the mother.  
 
I. 
Eliminating exceptions for the health of the pregnant person will lead to 
physical injury and death, and may cause maternal care provider shortages.  
 
The proposed rule, which includes a narrow exception only to save the life of the mother -- 
defined as “when a physician certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the 
fetus were carried to term” -- is unclear and ambiguous. It will force providers to prioritize 
considerations of criminal or civil penalties over the health of their patients.5 Substantial delays 
in care will result in unnecessary injuries, damaged fertility capabilities, and, in some cases, the 
death of pregnant people.   
 
Since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, healthcare providers across the country 
repeatedly are expressing concern and confusion about what services they can provide in 
states with severe abortion restrictions and bans. Doctors are reporting being forced to delay 
care for patients until the pregnant person is at risk of death or permanent injury, such as sepsis 
or hemorrhaging, in order to avoid legal repercussions for providing care.6 These precautions 
are resulting in significant complications that place the pregnant person’s life, health, and future 
fertility in serious jeopardy.  
 
In Texas, a woman with a nonviable pregnancy was denied an abortion due to the state abortion 
ban and later developed a life-threatening infection that caused scarring and a permanent 
blockage in one of her fallopian tubes.7 In Georgia, another woman visited a hospital after 
experiencing a rare complication from an abortion pill and was denied care for 20 hours. Instead 
of providing a dilation and curettage (D&C), a routine procedure to expel fetal tissue, doctors 
delayed the surgery for fear of violating a new Georgia law outlawing the procedure with a 
punishment of up to 10 years of prison.8 Thurman, the mother of a six-year-old, died.   
 
Given the health risks for patients and legal risks for providers, obstetrician-gynecologists 
(OBGYNs) may choose to leave the VA health system entirely. States with restrictive abortion 
laws have already felt these impacts. Sixty percent of doctors surveyed who practice under 
abortion bans reported considering moving, while eleven percent already relocated to states 
with greater protections for reproductive care.9 If VA clinicians follow this trend, pregnant 
veterans and their beneficiaries are likely to lack access to the resources, care and providers 
that support a healthy pregnancy.  
 
 
II. 
The proposed rule risks both the physical and mental health safety of 
veterans, including survivors of military sexual trauma.

Gynecologists' Perceived Impacts of Post–Dobbs v Jackson State Abortion Bans.

7 Tawkik, N. (2023, June 17). She was denied an abortion in Texas - then she almost died. BBC. 
https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-65935189

Experts Say This Mother’s Death Was Preventable. ProPublica. 
https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-abortion-ban-amber-thurman-death  
9 Sabbath, E. L., McKetchnie, S. M., Arora, K., S., & Buchbinder M. (2024, January 17). US Obstetrician-
Gynecologists' Perceived Impacts of Post–Dobbs v Jackson State Abortion Bans. 
2024;7;(1):e2352109. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.52109.   

Veterans are already more likely to experience mental health conditions and sexual assault 
stemming from their service. By eliminating reproductive health care options, the VA will 
severely harm servicemembers and veterans’ overall health.  
 
One in three women veterans report having experienced military sexual trauma (MST) during 
their service.10 In addition to physical health issues that may arise as a result of sexual assault 
or rape, such as injury or sexually transmitted infections (STIs), VA medical record data 
indicates that post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression and other mood disorders, and 
substance abuse are frequent diagnoses associated with MST.11 Being denied reproductive 
care as a victim of rape or intimate partner violence can further compound adverse mental 
health outcomes, such as depression, anxiety, PTSD and even suicide attempts.12  
 
The proposed rule would eliminate reproductive options for such veterans, forcing sexual 
assault victims to endure additional trauma, and in some cases, forced motherhood. Giving birth 
after rape has been associated with a unique form of PTSD called Rape Trauma Syndrome. A 
study of women previously subjected to rape found that rape trauma can be reactivated during 
childbirth, introducing feelings of being “dirtied, alienated and reduced to just a body.”13 
 
Women who are denied an abortion are more likely to face serious complications toward the 
end of pregnancy and can experience higher levels of anxiety.14 This is particularly concerning 
because veterans experience high rates of mental health conditions, including PTSD, which can 
contribute to increased pregnancy risks, including pre-term birth, preeclampsia and gestational 
diabetes.15 Denying female veterans access to the full range of reproductive health care -- 
including abortion care even in cases of rape, incest, and to protect the health of the pregnant 
person -- will place the health of veterans at unnecessary risk and fail to fulfill the VA’s 
commitment to support the health and well-being of all veterans.  
 
 
III. 
The proposed rule will impose unfair and detrimental financial burdens on 
veterans and their families.  
 
As of 2023, an estimated 400,000 female veterans live in states that have banned or are likely 
to ban abortion.16 Without the federal protection for abortion in cases of rape, incest or the 
health of the mother, the proposed rule will further limit access to care for veterans in restrictive 
states. In 2023, nearly one in five patients seeking abortion care traveled out of state.17 If the 
proposed rule is enacted, veterans may be forced to travel to states with protections for

https://www.guttmacher.org/2023/12/high-toll-us-abortion-bans-nearly-one-five-patients-now-traveling-
out-state-abortion-care.  

abortions to access necessary care, paying out-of-pocket and abandoning trusted healthcare 
providers who are familiar with their unique medical history and treatment.  
 
This imposes a large financial burden, requiring pregnant individuals to take time off work, find 
childcare and incur travel and lodging costs. Before the Dobbs. v. Jackson Women’s Health 
Organization ruling, estimated travel time for military personnel to the nearest abortion facility 
was 40.4 minutes, but post-Dobbs, estimated travel time increased to nearly four hours.18 This 
can be further complicated when states require counseling and waiting periods before patients 
can receive abortions, necessitating additional out-of-state travel. As of July 2025, 23 states 
require a waiting period between receiving counseling and an abortion.19 If veterans cannot 
afford to seek care outside the VA system, they may face high emergency care costs should 
pregnancy complications arise or health conditions deteriorate.  
 
Severe restrictions on abortion can exacerbate poor mental health outcomes, retraumatize 
victims of sexual assault, and lead to injuries, damaged fertility, and deaths that could have 
otherwise been prevented. 
 
To ensure that veterans and their loved ones can access safe, timely and necessary healthcare, 
we call on the VA to rescind this proposed rule and protect and preserve the wellbeing of our 
nation’s veterans.
